articles.title: Pre-emptive integration analysis: stop putting knowledge into your agents' context, watch their work instead
articles.excerpt: Part of the write-ups behind my Build Stuff 2026 talk, Control Your Fate at the Metal, Vilnius, 2 December. For a year, most of our effort went into getting knowledge into agents' context: summaries o…
articles.body: Part of the write-ups behind my Build Stuff 2026 talk, Control Your Fate at the Metal , Vilnius, 2 December. For a year, most of our effort went into getting knowledge into agents' context: summaries of every file, insights from earlier sessions, briefings on every prompt, notes on every command. The last parts of this series measured what came of it. Reach went up, and behaviour didn't change. Even my own corrections, captured as rules and fired at the moment they apply, didn't cut the repeats in the first days. They went up . One thing did work, and it isn't a context feature at all. What worked: watching the branches I run many agents at once, each on its own issue branch in its own worktree, across six repositories.
articles.author: Kent Alstad

articles.title: Heads of Security: Defending Against Prompt Injection by Gating Attention
articles.excerpt: Heads of Security: Defending Against Prompt Injection by Gating Attention Indirect prompt injection is what happens when an LLM agent reads a web page, an email, or a tool result and mistakes attacker…
articles.body: Heads of Security: Defending Against Prompt Injection by Gating Attention Indirect prompt injection is what happens when an LLM agent reads a web page, an email, or a tool result and mistakes attacker-planted text for a command from its user. A new paper from researchers at Imperial College London, the Tübingen AI Center and others, Heads of Security: Learned Attention Gates Improve Prompt Injection Robustness (arXiv, 27 Oct 2026), attacks the problem at a surprisingly low level: it trains a small set of per-head attention gates rather than fine-tuning the model's weights. This post walks through how the mechanism works, what the numbers show, and where the authors say it stops helping.
articles.author: Prabhakar Chaudhary

articles.title: Which SSH clients support MCP in 2026
articles.excerpt: A handful of SSH clients and terminals support MCP now, but "support MCP" means three different things, and the difference is what you actually care about: Built-in MCP server — the client exposes you…
articles.body: A handful of SSH clients and terminals support MCP now, but "support MCP" means three different things, and the difference is what you actually care about: Built-in MCP server — the client exposes your hosts as MCP tools an external agent can call (Conduit, XPipe, VibeShell, Termalin). MCP client — the app's own in-terminal agent can use other MCP servers (Warp). Community bridge or plugin — a third-party add-on exposes the app's sessions (Tabby, MobaXterm, Termius). Disclosure: we build Termalin , one of the entries below. Facts checked October 14, 2026 — this moves monthly, so check each vendor's page before you commit.

articles.excerpt: JavaScript is a legendary programming language. Created in the mid-1990s in just 10 days, it was born during the browser wars, when Netscape was trying to deliver a fatal blow to Microsoft. As we all…
articles.body: JavaScript is a legendary programming language. Created in the mid-1990s in just 10 days, it was born during the browser wars, when Netscape was trying to deliver a fatal blow to Microsoft. As we all know, that didn't exactly work out as planned… Today, some people love JavaScript, others hate it, and some just make fun of it. But the truth is, the modern web simply wouldn't exist without it! Over the years, JavaScript has gone through countless revolutions. Its capabilities today are almost incomparable to what the language could do back in the 1990s. There's just one tiny problem… Every change to the language has to take into account the fact that millions of websites out there still rely on old JavaScript behavior.

articles.title: My Manager Doesn't Understand Me. Are You Sure?
articles.excerpt: "My manager doesn't understand what I'm saying." I've heard this sentence many times. After meetings, in 1:1s, in channels the manager isn't in. I've said it myself, more than once. These days I hear…
articles.body: "My manager doesn't understand what I'm saying." I've heard this sentence many times. After meetings, in 1:1s, in channels the manager isn't in. I've said it myself, more than once. These days I hear it from both sides. I'm a lead: I report to an engineering manager, and six engineers across three teams work with me. Some days I'm the one shouting that something ahead looks wrong. Other days I'm the one who hears the shout and keeps the course anyway. Sitting in both seats has made one thing clearer to me. This sentence is rarely a diagnosis. It's usually a conclusion we reach too early, and this post is about what to do before reaching it. One sentence, three different problems When we say "my manager doesn't get it," one of three things has usually happened: The signal didn't land.

articles.title: Astronauts deploy solar array on 100th US spacewalk by International Space Station crew members
articles.excerpt: NASA astronaut Anil Menon and Joshua Kutryk of the Canadian Space Agency deployed a new solar array on Thursday (Oct. 29) during a seven-hour spacewalk outside the International Space Station.
articles.body: Two astronauts successfully installed and deployed the second-to-last upgraded solar array for the International Space Station (ISS) during the 100th U.S. spacewalk from the orbiting outpost. Anil Menon of NASA and Joshua Kutryk of the Canadian Space Agency (CSA), both ISS Expedition 75 crewmates, completed the 7-hour-and-11-minute extravehicular activity (EVA) at 3:08 p.m. EDT (1908 GMT) on Thursday (Oct. 29). The spacewalk began and ended inside the U.S. Quest airlock, with both astronauts wearing NASA's extravehicular mobility unit (EMU) spacesuits. It was the first spacewalk by a Canadian astronaut since April 2019, when David Saint-Jacques ventured into the void with NASA's Anne McClain.

articles.title: Square Enix should never make a Final Fantasy game without turn-based combat again
articles.excerpt: Final Fantasy Resonance is everything Square Enix's RPG series has struggled to achieve ove the last decade, and it should guide the series' future
articles.body: I had few expectations going into Final Fantasy Resonance , the premium game based on Square Enix's mobile gacha Brave Exvius . Those expectations lowered in the first 10 hours, thanks to its frankly atrocious writing. But after clearing most of the story and approaching the endgame, I find I've changed stances entirely. Resonance is everything Final Fantasy has struggled to achieve over the better part of two decades — confident, innovative, engaging, and, most importantly, completely and unashamedly itself. It's the blueprint Square Enix needs to follow for the series' future.
articles.author: Josh Broadwell

articles.title: 'Crystal Lake' is great, but nothing tops the space horror shenanigans of 'Jason X'
articles.excerpt: The Voorhees legend continues in Crystal Lake, but Jason X remains the Citizen Kane of this franchise.
articles.body: Peacock's "Crystal Lake" takes the story of the Voorhees family back to the beginning. It's a full-circle moment revisiting Pamela Voorhees (Linda Cardellini), who's the real star of 1980's "Friday the 13th" and the catalyst for all the murder and mayhem. While it's a welcome shake-up to the timeline of the horror franchise, nothing tops the originality of the slasher-in-space spectacle known as "Jason X". It was 2001, and the "Friday the 13th" franchise had hit a bit of a snag. Audiences had seen Jason Voorhees go everywhere from Crystal Lake to Manhattan and Hell, but where else could this hockey-masked killer go? Screenwriter Todd Farmer had the answer: space . "Jason X" says the quiet part out loud: Jason (Kane Hodder) can't die.

articles.title: NASA-funded Study Details One of Oldest Mars Meteorites Ever Found
articles.excerpt: When a rose-colored meteorite was found in the Sahara Desert in 2022, no one knew how old it was or where it came from. Not until NASA-funded scientists age-dated its minerals did they realize the nea…
articles.body: 5 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) Called Teghaza 001, this rose-colored rock is one of the most ancient Martian meteorites ever found on Earth. Credit: © Darryl Pitt / Maine Mineral & Gem Museum When a rose-colored meteorite was found in the Sahara Desert in 2022, no one knew how old it was or where it came from. Not until NASA-funded scientists age-dated its minerals did they realize the nearly 2-pound (800-gram) rock was a piece of Mars that formed more than 4.1 billion years ago, making it one of the oldest Martian meteorites ever found. Named Teghaza 001 after the salt plain in Mali where it was discovered, the meteorite is one of roughly 435 from the Red Planet.

articles.body: Photo of Troy Asher NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman has named Troy Asher director of the agency’s Armstrong Flight Research Center in Edwards, California. Asher, a veteran test pilot and aerospace engineer with decades of experience in flight research and operations, has served as the center’s acting director since March. “Troy has spent his career pushing the boundaries of flight, both at the controls of experimental aircraft and leading the teams that make these missions possible,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman.

articles.title: Cosmic graveyard of zombie planets offers a grisly warning about our own solar system's fate
articles.excerpt: Two zombie exoplanets that rose from the grave to shuffle through the gory remains of their fellow planets may just agree with these immortal words from horror maestro Stephen King.
articles.body: "Sometimes dead is better." Who can forget the immortal words of Jud Crandall, delivered by the incomparable Fred Gwynne in the 1989 film adaptation of Stephen King's Pet Sematary? Turns out Crandall could have been talking about somewhere just as otherworldly as the cursed Chumash burial ground at the heart of one of King's most terrifying works of fiction. That's because astronomers have discovered two husks of two zombie planets shuffling through the gory remains of what was once their planetary neighbors around a long-deceased star, or white dwarf. The shattered planets were revealed by a clear gap in the debris around the white dwarf J1328−1450, located around 1,600 light-years away from Earth.

articles.body: 2 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) The Quantum-Enabled Predictive Preclinical NAMs for Toxicity and Safety (QuSAFE) Challenge, a collaboration between the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and NASA, advances quantum-enabled sensing for in vitro NAMs, such as organoids and microphysiological systems (MPS), to improve drug safety while reducing animal use. In vitro NAMs, such as organoids and microphysiological systems (MPS), can generate human-relevant data for drug development and safety evaluation. However, conventional assays and imaging are often noisy, invasive, and not sensitive enough.
